post_copy:
750 camera feeds is the ceiling Anchorage funded for its police crime center.

It opened last September with about 15 cameras and one employee.

Seven days left. Three members introduced surveillance rules on August 18th. On September 1st they share a table with a roughly $600,000 equipment contract.

The AI in the center today reads plates. The chief says police don't use facial recognition. The rule would require Assembly approval before AI powered tracking or identification is added.

Inside, the launch state, the four proposed rules and the retention clocks that are practice and not code.

A rule is cheap to write while the machine is small. If the money passes and the rules don't, what should happen to the feeds nobody has switched on?

#AnchorageAssembly #PolicingTech #AKPolitics

first_comment:
Sources, primary first.

Anchorage Daily News opinion by Assembly member Sydney Scout, ordinance co-sponsor, on public safety and civil liberties, August 20th. https://www.adn.com/opinions/2026/08/20/opinion-public-safety-cannot-come-at-the-expense-of-civil-liberties/

Anchorage Daily News, on the proposed surveillance expansion and the members who want privacy protections first, August 20th. https://www.adn.com/alaska-news/anchorage/2026/08/20/anchorage-police-may-expand-surveillance-capabilities-some-assembly-members-want-privacy-protections-first/

Alaska Public Media, on the Assembly weighing the police surveillance upgrade, August 21st. https://alaskapublic.org/news/anchorage/2026-08-21/as-anchorage-assembly-weighs-police-surveillance-upgrade-some-members-want-privacy-protections-first

Alaska's News Source, on the police request to upgrade real time crime monitoring, August 5th. https://www.alaskasnewssource.com/2026/08/05/anchorage-police-seeking-upgrades-real-time-crime-monitoring/

One caveat, stated plainly. The ordinance text and its AO number were not publicly reachable while this deck was built, so every description of the ordinance here comes from a reporter or from its co-sponsor, never from statute. Slide 06 uses the co-sponsor's own wording for the AI provision and says so on the slide.

Every Alaska AI decision this page tracks, with its live deadline, sits at https://alaskaaihq.com

If you have read the ordinance itself or sat in the August 21st work session, add what is missing here.

slides.headline: 750 feeds funded. About 15 running. Hearing September 1st.
labels: 750 IS DESIGNED FEED CAPACITY (C07). ABOUT 15 IS THE CAMERA COUNT AT LAUNCH (C11). DIFFERENT UNITS.

slides.headline: One employee. About 15 cameras.
slides.body: The Real Time Crime Center opened at police properties and Town Square Park. The Assembly had already approved $11.8 million for a system designed to stream up to 750 feeds. The room was one person.

slides.headline: Most of the cameras already exist.
slides.body: The center is separate from dispatch. It is used once a call comes in, to help officers respond, the police chief says. (C33)
labels: GIVEN, NOT TAKEN · RESIDENTS, NOT CAMERAS (C10)
THESE DO NOT ADD TO 750. DIFFERENT UNITS, NO SUM. (C07)

slides.headline: The AI in this system reads plates.
labels: Object recognition on the license plate readers, the police chief says.
Facial recognition. The department does not use it, the chief says.
THE ASSEMBLY PLACED STRICT LIMITS ON IT IN 2023 (C21, C26)
Whether object recognition data can be transmitted through the system at all.
THE CHIEF SAYS THAT IS UNKNOWN (C25)
SOLID, IN FORCE. DASHED, NOT YET OR UNKNOWN.
STATE, NOT SIZE. COLUMNS ARE EQUAL.

slides.body: "Let's put this into code now, so that when power changes, when the political winds shift, as they always do, we have protections for the people, no matter who is overseeing and implementing the system."

slides.headline: Four rules, none of them law yet.
labels: A case number for every search of surveillance data.
Deletion after two weeks, unless it is evidence in an active investigation.
No footage to out of state or federal agencies without a warrant.
Plate readers only for traffic enforcement and justifiable tracking, like missing kids or stolen vehicles.
Assembly approval before adding new surveillance capabilities, including AI powered tracking or identification technology.
CO-SPONSOR SYDNEY SCOUT'S OWN DESCRIPTION, NOT THE TEXT
THREE PUBLISHED ACCOUNTS WORD THIS PROVISION THREE WAYS. THE ORDINANCE TEXT IS NOT PUBLIC. (C20)

slides.headline: The clock barely changes. Who can change it does.
slides.body: "When my constituents ask, 'What are we collecting? Who can see it? How long do we keep it?' Anchorage code can't answer any of those questions."
labels: TRAFFIC FOOTAGE · OVERWRITTEN, 3 TO 5 DAYS · PRACTICE (C13)
PROPOSED IN CODE · DELETED, TWO WEEKS · NOT IN FORCE (C15)
TODAY THESE ARE DEPARTMENT PRACTICE, NOT CODE.

slides.headline: The money and the rule arrive on the same day.
slides.body: Roughly $600,000 to ThunderCat Technology for video displays, sound equipment and video processing technology, from fine and forfeiture funds. The system it upgrades was approved at $11.8 million (C05).
labels: ON THE TABLE SEPTEMBER 1ST (C02, C03, C04)

slides.headline: The rule is still cheap to write.
slides.body: Ask your Assembly member which of the four they will vote for on September 1st.

aftercare: Post it today if the morning allows. Tuesday through Thursday, 8 to 11am Alaska time, is the strongest window, and the caption says seven days left, which is only true on August 25th. If it slips to Wednesday, the caption's count line has to move with it.

Paste the sources comment within 60 seconds of posting, before the first reader lands. It carries the caveat that the ordinance text was not publicly reachable, and that caveat should never arrive after a reader has already asked.
Reply to every comment in the first 60 to 90 minutes. That window decides how far the deck travels, and this topic will pull both police supporters and privacy readers.

If a commenter says the crime center already runs facial recognition, correct it with the chief's own words. The AI in the system today reads plates, the department says it does not use facial recognition, and the chief says it is unknown whether object recognition data can move through the system at all.

If someone asks for the ordinance's exact wording, say plainly that the text was not public when this was built and that slide 06 quotes the co-sponsor's description. Do not paraphrase it into something firmer.
Watch the Assembly agenda for September 1st once it posts. A postponement, an amendment or an AO number is the follow up post, and it is also the docket update.
Note saves and comments at 48 hours. This is the first deck built on a countdown structure with a cold number opener, so the number matters to the caption ledger.
editor_notes_for_email: The ordinance text and its AO number were never publicly reachable during this run. anchorage.legistar.com returned an invalid parameters error and muni.org carried no September 1st agenda, so no AO number appears in the deck, the caption or the first comment. Every description of the ordinance in this deck is a description by a reporter or by its co-sponsor, never statutory language, and nothing about the ordinance is set in quotation marks as the ordinance's own words. Slide 06 prints Assembly member Sydney Scout's wording for the AI provision, taken from her signed op-ed, with her attribution directly beneath it and the C20 footnote on the same slide saying three published accounts word the provision three ways. The phrase 'human feature recognition' is the ADN reporter's sentence rather than the ordinance's, so it appears nowhere in the deck, the caption or the sources comment, deliberately.
